# How to use this workbook {.unnumbered}

This book is a series of things you do, not a series of things you read. The
reading is there to make the doing possible, and it's kept as short as that
allows.

Here's how it's built, so you can decide how to spend your time on it.

## Every chapter has the same six parts

A chapter opens with a **question** you can't yet answer. Then comes the
**concept**, which is the smallest amount of theory that makes the next part
possible. Then the **walkthrough**, where the work is done in front of you with
every result printed on the page. Then the **exercises**, where you do it, and
each one names the thing you'll have at the end. Then **if it breaks**, which
lists the specific ways it goes wrong and what to do about each. Then a
**checkpoint**, so you can tell whether to move on.

When you're short on time, the walkthrough and the exercises are the chapter.
The concept section will still be there next week.

## What you need

A browser. A Google account, from Chapter 4 onward. About three hours a week.

Nothing in this book is installed. There's no terminal, no package manager, and
no moment where the instructions stop working because a version number moved.
The one install command in the whole book appears in Chapter 17, and the book
says so when it arrives.

Every dataset used here is already in the repository, so no chapter depends on
a download working while you're sitting there. Where the book does ask you to
fetch something, the size is stated in the sentence that asks.

## Time estimates, and what they assume

Every exercise carries a time in minutes. Those numbers assume you're typing
the code rather than pasting it, that you'll stop to read at least one database
record properly, and that something will go wrong once.

If an exercise takes you twice its estimate, that's within range. If it takes
you five times, something is actually stuck, and the *if it breaks* section is
the right place to look before the internet is.

Most chapters run seven to nine pages, which is one comfortable sitting. The
four that open the book are shorter, and Chapter 24, where the whole project
runs start to finish, is the longest thing in here.

## What to do when you're stuck

In this order, and the order matters.

1. Read the last line of the error message. Not the first line, and not the
   whole block. The last line is the one that says what went wrong.
2. Check the *if it breaks* section of the chapter you're in. If the error is
   listed there, it's listed with a fix.
3. Check the error index at the back of the book, which maps every error
   message this book explains to the page that explains it.
4. Compare your code against the printed version, character by character, on
   the line the error names. Roughly half the time it's a quotation mark, a
   bracket, or a letter.
5. Search the exact error message, with your own filenames and variable names
   taken out. Chapter 16 covers how to do that well.

Chapter 16 is the one to read early if you get stuck often. It's about reading
errors, and it's the longest chapter in Part 2 for a reason.

## Type the code

You'll be tempted to copy and paste, and sometimes you should. But the first
time you meet anything new, type it.

The reason isn't discipline. It's that typing produces small errors, and small
errors are how you learn what the error messages mean while nothing is at
stake. A reader who has never seen a `SyntaxError` in a calm moment reads it as
a verdict when it finally shows up in the middle of something they care about.

## Where everything lives

The code, the data, the answers to every exercise, and the source of this book
are all at `github.com/rikhinkavuru/NoLabRequired`. Chapter 3 prints that
address, and it's the only full web address in the body of the book. Everywhere
else you get a bare domain. Every exact address this book took a number from is
collected in the index at the back, with the date it was last checked. Printed
links go stale, and a book that scatters them through its body text ages badly.

If something here is wrong, the repository is where to say so.
